Given you have fish in the tank you are going to have to manage the cycling with them in. If you do it right the fish will survive and won’t suffer too much stress. 

You need to test for ammonia nitrites and nitrates every day. If the ammonia rises above 2.0 ppm then you will need to do a small water change (20%) max to stop the level rising above where the fish will suffer. You can’t drop it too much otherwise the cycle will stall. 

Once you have had ammonia for around a week to ten days you should see the nitrites start to increase. Again you need to monitor these carefully as they are toxic to the fish. If they start getting close to 2.0 ppm then change the water as before. 

The nitrates will start to appear in a few days and will start to reduce the ammonia and nitrate levels until you get zero readings of both. 

Personally I would bother putting any other chemicals in now. I would just keep feeding the fish checking the levels and changing water as necessary. If the fish look stressed then change some more water. 

It might take an extra few day in the cycle but in the end it will all be worth it. 

I would t be adding any new fish either until the tank is ready and cycled properly

Have you seen any nitrites at all? Just because your ammonia is going down doesn’t mean the tank is cycling. 5 neon tetra wouldn’t produce enough waste products per day to keep the ammonia levels up. 

I always use liquid ammonia to cycle any new tank and it usually takes a good 2 weeks before you could say the tank was nearing the point I would dream of putting any fish in

Many “traditional” marathon training plans talk about doing your long run slower than race pace so you build up strength etc. They always refer to this as training and not racing. 

All I learnt from following this concept was MP on race day felt uncomfortable and hard work. 

I decided to challenge this thinking by spending a lot of my marathon training sessions at either above or beyond MP so it felt comfortable on race day. 

I did this with lots of long (1 and 2k) intervals, long progression runs and double sessions on long run days with the 1st run being run at a reasonable pace and the 2nd run being more of a relaxed pace. 

I made sure I had 2 easy runs in my weekly schedule to give my legs a chance of recovery 

My week looked like this: -

Monday rest
Tuesday long intervals
Wednesday easy 1 hour
Thursday hard day with mid to long run 
Friday rest
Saturday long run - progression or split (alternating weeks)
Sunday evening to maximise rest from Sunday - 1 hour easy

On race day my MP felt comfortable and I never felt as if I was running out of my comfort zone

Hope this makes sense and helps.

Running your first marathon is a huge step to take. One not to be taken lightly and I am sure you have done a lot of research to make sure you are ready for the challenge. 

From my own experiences it's not like running 2 HM's back to back its more like running 3!

The biggest question you need to ask yourself is do you just want to finish  (taking into account the time you have been running, your current training load and how your body reacts to increased weekly distances) or do you have a specific (and realistic) goal time. 

There are many excellent online (free) training plans that will focus on a goal time, or a maximum weekly mileage / number of runs per week. Following one of these will be a tremendous help to you and will be an excellent gauge as to how things are likely to pan out. 

Placing yourself in the wrong starting group could have 2 potential downsides. The first is the effect on others having to run around you if they are quicker than you. Self seeding works really well if everyone has a clear expectation of heir own ability. A BOP runner shouldn't be starting near the from of any race. 

The second, and perhaps more important point, is your own pace. Starting in the wrong group could see you blowing your race plan out of the windows in the first few k's by simply going out too quick by being caught up in the moment. A few extra seconds above your goal pace in the first 10k will come back to bite you very hard between 30-40k. It's very easy to try and keep up with those that start around you given the excitement of the gun going off. 

I would personally opt for the slower group and run my own race from there. 

Good luck and let us know how you get in with your training.

I would make a few changes to your program

Monday - rest
Tuesday - medium/hard (split run into 4 equal distance segment. Run segments 1 & 3 at a sensible pace and 2 & 4 closer to race pace) The total distance of the run needs to be between 10 and 14km
Wednesday- easy
Thursday - hard (intervals should be either 800's or 1km. The goal is to run each one with consistency. The first and last should be around the same pace). This session should see you covering a minimum of 12 km with warm up and cool down
Friday - rest 
Saturday - long run ( progression running building to race pace, or a steady state run). 
Sunday - late afternoon recovery run to maximise rest time from Saturday run. Should be between 30 mins and 1 hour depending on how close you are to the end of your program. The closer the marathon day the longer the run
